summary: The page has two parts. First, it confirms that the Chamber of the Lambs was in the southwest, resolving the contradiction concerning the location of the chamber where the shewbread was prepared. The objection that all turns must be to the right is answered: that rule applies during Temple service, not to a mere reckoning. Second, the High Priest may choose first which offering to sacrifice and which portion to eat. A baraita says he takes one of the two Shavuot loaves and four or five shewbread loaves; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says he always takes five. Abaye resolves the baraita's apparent inconsistency by explaining that the Rabbis concede that it is inappropriate to give the High Priest a piece of a loaf.

display.title: Operational rule, not descriptive rule: why 'turn right' does not govern the chamber's corner
display.whats: Confirmation that the Chamber of the Lambs was in the southwest. A brief objection based on the rule that all turns must be to the right is answered: that rule applies during Temple service, while here the leftward description is only a reckoning and no priest actually followed that route.
display.hint: Why does the rule that all turns must be to the right not prevent a tanna from describing the chambers via the left?

learning.learnerQuestion: If priests are required to always turn right during service, shouldn't that same rule dictate the order in which the Talmud lists Temple chambers?
learning.coreTension: How can one tanna envision the chambers via the left when the rule requires all turns to be made only to the right?
learning.coreMove: The Gemara distinguishes two different things 'turning right' could mean: an operational halakha governing how a kohen physically moves during the Temple service, versus a literary convention for how a tanna sequences chamber locations in a description. Since kol piyot only governs the former, it cannot be imported to constrain or contradict the latter.
learning.resolution: The SW corner placement stands confirmed; kol piyot does not apply to descriptive chamber-counting, only to actual priestly movement during service.

takeaway.text: A rule governing how an action is physically performed does not automatically govern how that same domain is described or counted in a text - operational halakha and literary convention are different categories.

learning.ahaMoment: Context matters: the 'always right' rule is operational (what priests do during service), not descriptive (how a tanna counts rooms). Applying it to room-listing order is a category error.
learning.learningBlocker: Learners who just met kol piyot as a Temple-service halakha try to apply it everywhere a right turn appears, including chamber-listing order - but a rule about how kohanim walk during the rite says nothing about how a tanna sequences a written description.
learning.memoryAnchor: SW corner confirmed. 'Always right' binds kohanim during actual service; it says nothing about the order a tanna lists rooms in a description.

argumentFlow.label: SW corner confirmed for Chamber of the Lambs
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Final determination: the Chamber of the Lambs was in the southwest corner. If it were in the northwest, the Chamber of the Seals would interpose between it and the shewbread chamber, so Rav Huna's resolution would fail.

argumentFlow.label: Objection: How may the chambers be described via the left?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara objects that all turns should be made only to the right, whereas one tanna's reckoning describes the chambers via the left.

argumentFlow.label: Response: 'always right' applies to service movement, not counting
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The rule that priests always turn right applies when they are performing Temple service - walking around during rituals. It does not apply when scholars are theoretically listing or counting chamber locations.

sourceRefs.note: Limitation of the rightward-turn rule to service context

misconceptions.misconception: The 'all turns to the right' rule constrains how the Talmud describes or lists Temple chambers.
misconceptions.correction: It only constrains actual priestly movement during service; chamber-listing order in a tanna's description is a separate, unrelated convention.

visualizableElements.item: Diagram showing the Chamber of the Lambs in the southwest and contrasting rightward turns during Temple service with a leftward descriptive reckoning

quizSeeds.question: Why may a tanna enumerate the chambers leftward despite the rule that all turns must be to the right?
quizSeeds.answer: Kol piyot is an operational halakha governing how kohanim physically move during Temple service; it does not govern the order in which a tanna lists or describes chamber locations in a text.

quizSeeds.question: What two different things could 'turning right' mean in this sugya, and which one does kol piyot actually regulate?
quizSeeds.answer: It could mean a kohen's physical movement during service, or the literary order in which a tanna lists chambers. Kol piyot regulates only the first; chamber lists follow each tanna's own descriptive convention.

sugyot.finalRuling: Chamber of the Lambs = SW corner. 'All turns right' applies to service movement only.
prerequisiteKnowledge: The dispute over whether the Chamber of the Lambs was in the southwest or northwest
The 'all turns to the right' rule in Temple service

display.title: First portion, not a guaranteed half: the KG's Shewbread privilege
display.whats: Two topics. First: the High Priest may choose which offering to sacrifice and which sin-offering or guilt-offering to eat. Second: the baraita gives him one of the two Shavuot loaves and four or five Shewbread loaves. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says he always takes five, while the Rabbanan say he takes less than half.
display.hint: How can the baraita say that the High Priest takes one of the two Shavuot loaves, yet only four or five of the twelve shewbread loaves?

learning.learnerQuestion: If the High Priest's privilege is to take the first portion, why would he ever receive less than half the Shewbread loaves?
learning.coreTension: The KG's privilege seems to entitle him to half of the loaves, yet the Rabbanan hold that his portion of the Shewbread is only four or five loaves, less than half.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara tests the baraita's clauses against the dispute. One of two Shavuot loaves appears to follow Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's half-share rule; four or five Shewbread loaves appears to follow the Rabbanan, who give less than half; and the final clause explicitly gives Rabbi's ruling of five. Abaye instead assigns the first and middle clauses to the Rabbanan: although their share would be less than one Shavuot loaf, they concede that it is inappropriate to give the KG a piece, so he receives a whole loaf.
learning.resolution: The dispute remains between Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who says the KG always takes five, and the Rabbanan, who give him less than half. Abaye reads the first and middle clauses of the baraita as Rabbanan, with their concession that the KG receives a whole Shavuot loaf.

takeaway.text: A privilege to take 'the first portion' does not itself guarantee half of the total: the Rabbanan give the KG less than half of the Shewbread, while Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says he always takes five.

learning.ahaMoment: Although the Rabbanan give the KG less than half, they concede that he takes one whole Shavuot loaf, since it is inappropriate to give the High Priest a piece of a loaf.
learning.learningBlocker: Learners may assume that 'takes the first portion' means the KG must receive half. The baraita instead records the Rabbanan's less-than-half position, while granting him one whole Shavuot loaf because giving him a piece would be inappropriate.
learning.memoryAnchor: KG chooses first and takes first. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: always five Shewbread loaves. Rabbanan: less than half, four or five; but one whole Shavuot loaf, because a piece is inappropriate.

argumentFlow.label: Mishna: KG sacrifices first and takes first
argumentFlow.speaker: Mishna
argumentFlow.text: The High Priest's privilege: he may choose first which burnt-offering or meal-offering to sacrifice and which sin-offering or guilt-offering to eat.

argumentFlow.label: Shewbread loaf count varies: 4 or 5
argumentFlow.speaker: Baraita
argumentFlow.text: The KG receives either four or five of the twelve Shewbread loaves.

argumentFlow.label: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi vs Rabbanan on KG's loaf portion
argumentFlow.speaker: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi / Rabbanan
argumentFlow.text: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: the KG always takes five of the twelve Shewbread loaves, based on “for Aaron and his sons,” which gives half to Aaron and half to his sons. Rabbanan: the KG takes less than half, namely four or five loaves.

argumentFlow.label: How are the two Shavuot loaves handled?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The baraita says the KG takes one of the two Shavuot loaves, four or five of the Shewbread loaves, while Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says he always takes five. The Gemara asks whether its first and last clauses follow Rabbi while its middle clause follows the Rabbanan.

misconceptions.misconception: The KG receives exactly half of the twelve Shewbread loaves.
misconceptions.correction: Per the Rabbanan, the KG takes less than half of the Shewbread—four or five loaves. They nevertheless give him one whole Shavuot loaf because it is inappropriate to give the High Priest a piece.

visualizableElements.item: Shewbread distribution: 12 loaves, of which the KG takes four or five. From the two Shavuot loaves, he takes one whole loaf.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: the KG always takes five of the twelve Shewbread loaves. Rabbanan: the KG takes four or five. Two columns comparing the positions.

quizSeeds.question: What is the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the Rabbanan about the KG's Shewbread portion?
quizSeeds.answer: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds that the KG always takes five of the twelve Shewbread loaves. The Rabbanan hold that he takes four or five loaves.

quizSeeds.question: How does Abaye resolve the apparent inconsistency within the baraita's own wording about the KG's portion?
quizSeeds.answer: He reads the baraita's opening and middle clauses as following the Rabbanan. They concede that the KG takes one whole Shavuot loaf because it is inappropriate to give him a piece; the closing clause follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.

sugyot.finalRuling: Disputed: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says the KG always takes five Shewbread loaves, while the Rabbanan hold that he takes less than half. Abaye reads the first and middle clauses of the baraita as Rabbanan, who concede that the KG receives a whole Shavuot loaf because giving him a piece is inappropriate.

glossary.en: The two loaves offered on the festival of Shavuot; the High Priest may take one of them.
The two loaves offered on the festival of Shavuot, one of which the High Priest may take.

rashiTranslations.en: 'If you say, granted' - the tanna of Tamid himself, who taught 'the chamber of the lambs
is in the northwest,' agrees that it was more toward the southwest, but
he phrased his mishna according to how it appeared to his eye - 'and one coming from the south, it appears to him from the north' -
and he really does begin counting from the southwestern corner; this is what answers
the difficulty of the showbread chamber against the showbread chamber, that it comes to be
in the southeast, as is taught in Middot,
so that they do not contradict each other. How so? The chamber of the lambs
in the southwest, the chamber of the seals
when you go by way of the left, in the northwest
- the chamber of the hearth in the north-
east; the chamber of the showbread in the south-
east. 'But if you say' - that specifically
the tanna taught the chamber of the lambs at the northwest
corner - in the end, what did you answer for the showbread
chamber? For when he counts by way of the left, the chamber
of the showbread would be in the southwest, according to
his count. 'But did the master not say' - further on (daf
58b). 'From two loaves' - of Shavuot
'Four or five' - on each and every Shabbat,
and further on it explains when four and when
five. 'And it shall belong to Aaron and his sons' - it is written regarding the showbread
itself. 'Half to Aaron, etc.' -
even though there are twelve of them, there are
among them two loaves that are not divided,
as it goes on to explain. 'We come to the Rabbis' -
who say he does not take a half, for if he took
a half, he would take less than five, which he does not take. 'The first clause
and the middle clause are the Rabbis' - who say he does not take
a half, but rather less than half; and as for your difficulty from
the loaf of the two-loaves offering, which he takes whole,
the Rabbis concede that it is not proper conduct
to break it and give a broken piece to the High Priest
'And what' - the daf ends mid-word here; the comment (explaining 'four or five', when four and when five) continues on 18a.
